# Using ISLA {#sec-using}

**ISLA ships as one class with one recommended configuration, trained and
evaluated by the unified external-aerodynamics recipe; this chapter is the
operating manual.** It tells you which configuration to run and why, what
the model needs from your data, the two commands that train and evaluate
it, the learning-rate rule that lets it scale in width and depth, the
inference sampler that removes most of the draw noise at a fixed cell
budget, and what a step costs. Everything here is about ISLA unless an
option is named; the reasons behind each recommendation are in @sec-mt2 and
the evidence chapters, cited at the point where they apply.

## Which configuration {#sec-using-config}

Use **ISLA as shipped**: the relative frame, which has no origin, with the
RMS-pairwise-distance length unit. It is the class default, so `ISLA()` with
no arguments is it, and the recipe's `isla_surface.yaml` states the one
frame setting explicitly:

```yaml
model:
  _target_: physicsnemo.experimental.nn.ISLA
  out_scalars: 1        # pressure
  out_vectors: 1        # wall shear stress
  hidden: 192
  n_layers: 12
  n_slices: 256
  mlp_ratio: 4
  scale_mode: rms_distance    # length unit = measure-weighted RMS pairwise distance of the sample (the frame has no origin)
  geo_checkpoint: true        # rebuild per-slice geometry in backward: same numbers, half the memory
```

The configuration table below is the whole decision. ISLA has one frame,
preferred on principle (no center is estimated from the sample), and the
measurements that priced the alternatives left that preference unopposed on
accuracy: the similarity-gauge variant, before its removal, was within 2% of
ISLA at 435 cars, inside seed noise (@sec-nb-sgref-verdict). The removed
frame variants survive only in this book's collapsed diagnostic notes
(@sec-mt2-variants). The remaining rows are options on that one frame.

| configuration | recipe config | when to use | what you give up |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ISLA** (relative frame, RMS-pairwise-distance length unit, linear routing) | `isla_surface`, `isla_volume` | every new surface or interior task | nothing among ISLA's options; against GeoTransolver, nothing at 435 DrivAerML cars at the reporting protocol, up to 17% below full data on the cars and 27% on the 35-wing rung (@sec-scoreboard-200k) |
| cosine routing (`routing_norm: cosine`; the candidate default) | option on `isla_surface`, `isla_volume` | any width above 384 or depth above 24 layers, or any time a linear-routing lane reaches the mean-field plateau | nothing measured on DrivAerML: accuracy at the rule rates is within 1% of linear routing at widths 192 and 384 and 2% at 768, and the learning-rate ceiling is gone (@sec-using-lr); the same test on the wings is pending, so the default has not moved |
| query mass (`query_mass: source_total`, the default; `geometric_mean`) | option on `isla_volume`, `isla_volume_support` | interior tasks only: the routing weight the interior query tokens carry. The default gives them a learned fraction of the total boundary measure, so it is invariant to re-representing the same surface at another refinement; `geometric_mean` gives each query the mean boundary log-weight plus a learned offset, which depends on the refinement, and is the setting of the interior evidence lanes (@sec-interior) | nothing measured; the two have not been compared at the reporting protocol |
| total-measure unit (`scale_mode: total_measure`; marked for removal) | option on `isla_surface`, `isla_volume` | reproducing the evidence lanes trained under that unit, and nothing else | nothing measurable: within 1.3% of the default at 435 cars (@sec-nb-lenrms-verdict); not normalized, so it inherits any error in the weights' absolute scale, and divergent under refinement of a boundary whose area does not converge. Scheduled for removal once those lanes are retired |
| passive decoder (`query_independent: true`) | `isla_volume_support` | when the prediction at a point must not depend on which other points are queried | 3.0 to 3.7x in accuracy (@sec-query-independence) |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The legacy centered variant (removed)"}
The centered frame with a fixed length unit was the program's configuration
before the relative frame, and the recipe carried it as
`isla_surface_constant_gauge` for the diagnostic that shows what a
sample-estimated center costs (its error grows 12x under a 10:1
sampling-density bias at the exploration budget of 10,000 cells). The
centered frame, the similarity gauge and the constant reference length were
removed from the class and the recipe (@sec-nb-frame-cleanup); their
measurements stay in this book's diagnostic notes, their checkpoints no
longer load.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Checkpoints remember their configuration"}
Every checkpoint stores its constructor arguments, so a model saved under
any current option loads in the configuration that trained it; you never
have to recall which length unit a checkpoint used. ISLA keeps no
compatibility shims for its own pre-release history: a checkpoint that
names a removed option (the centered frame, the similarity gauge, the
constant reference length, or the research options removed earlier) does
not load, and the measurements made with such checkpoints are reported in
this book as measurements of a removed variant (@sec-nb-frame-cleanup,
@sec-nb-no-legacy-compat).
:::

## What the model needs from your data {#sec-using-inputs}

**ISLA takes four arrays per case, and the two that are easy to get wrong
are the measure weights, which must sum to the surface area, and the global
vector, which must be a unit direction.** The forward call is keyword-only,
so the recipe's `forward_kwargs:` mapping reads exactly as the call does.
For the surface task:

```yaml
forward_kwargs:
  points: interior.points                                  # (B, N, 3) sampled cell centroids ("interior" is the datapipe's name for the sampled point set, not the fluid domain)
  normals: boundaries.vehicle.cell_data.normals            # (B, N, 3) unit outward normals
  measure_weights: interior.point_data._effective_measure   # (B, N) area each sampled cell stands for
  global_vectors: global_data.U_inf_dir                    # (B, 1, 3) the freestream as a unit direction
```

Three of these need a word.

- **The measure weights must sum to the surface area.** When the recipe
  keeps $n$ of $N$ cells, each kept cell carries the Horvitz–Thompson weight,
  its area times $N/n$, so that the weights stand for the full surface at
  any `sampling_resolution`: the routing's quadrature sums, and the
  total-measure unit when that option is used, then read the surface area
  rather than the retained fraction of it (the default RMS-pairwise-distance
  unit normalizes the weights and is indifferent to the factor, but the
  quadrature sums are not). The surface
  dataset stores this in `interior.point_data._effective_measure`; the
  volume dataset uses `boundaries.vehicle.cell_data._effective_measure`
  through its `ComposeQuadratureMeasure` stage. Both are complete measures,
  including sampling corrections. Point measures carry their represented
  dimension and follow geometric scaling. Feeding raw sub-sampled areas shrinks the
  length unit by the kept fraction and moves every invariant out of its
  trained range.
- **The global vector must be a unit direction.** `ComputeFreestreamDirection`
  writes `U_inf_dir` from the physical velocity; the model normalizes it
  again internally and discards the magnitude. This is also the
  fair-comparison rule for every architecture in the book
  (@sec-fair-comparison): fed the physical velocity, GeoTransolver's global
  context routes to a single slice and loses 3.4 to 3.8x.
- **A speed or other magnitude that matters is a global scalar.** Set
  `n_global_scalars` and pass `global_scalars` of shape (B, S). No fixed power
  of the freestream speed is a physical law for every output (a pressure
  coefficient is degree zero, a dimensional pressure degree two), so the
  model learns the dependence like any other parameter.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Problems other than external aerodynamics"}
The architecture knows only that it was handed $K$ global directions and
$S$ global scalars. A buoyant flow passes gravity as its one direction; a
magnetized flow passes two; steady conduction with pinned temperatures
passes none (`n_global_vectors: 0`) and supplies the pinned values as
per-cell `boundary_scalars` (`n_boundary_scalars`). Each global direction
adds one seed cosine, one relational cosine and three vectors to the output
basis (@sec-mt2-inputs). The tests in `test_isla_global_inputs.py` cover
zero and two directions, global scalars, and the invariance of the output to
the magnitude of every global vector.
:::

## Training {#sec-using-train}

**Train at the recipe defaults, 200,000 sampled cells per case for 500
epochs at learning rate 1e-3, with no augmentation; the only setting that
needs thought is the learning rate when you leave width 192.** From the
recipe root:

```bash
# DrivAerML surface, ISLA (sampling_resolution defaults to 200,000 cells per case)
python src/train.py model=isla_surface dataset=drivaer_ml_surface \
    training.optimizer.lr=1e-3 compile=false

# DrivAerML interior: boundary -> volume, queries as interacting tokens with the signed distance.
# 5e-4, not 1e-3: with 200,000 boundary cells and 200,000 queries interacting, 1e-3 reaches the mean-field plateau
python src/train.py model=isla_volume dataset=drivaer_ml_volume_reference \
    training.optimizer.lr=5e-4 compile=false

# HiLiftAeroML surface (the 200,000-cell default again)
python src/train.py model=isla_surface dataset=highlift_surface \
    training.optimizer.lr=1e-3 compile=false training.num_epochs=200
```

The reporting protocol behind the evidence chapters' numbers is the recipe
default of 200,000 sampled cells per case (@sec-scoreboard-tokens), 500
epochs, bfloat16 autocast, no augmentation, learning rate 1e-3 at width
192, final-epoch checkpoint (@sec-protocol); every architecture is trained
at its own best rate. Numbers at the exploration budget of 10,000 cells per
case are labeled as such wherever they appear. ISLA needs no rotation
augmentation: the contracts make it exact, and a model trained in the
dataset's native frame predicts a car in any pose (@sec-pose).

### The learning-rate rule {#sec-using-lr}

**Under the default linear routing, set the learning rate to
$10^{-3} \times 192 / \mathrm{hidden} \times 12 / \mathrm{layers}$; under
`routing_norm: cosine` the ceiling behind that rule is gone on DrivAerML,
and the same expression is only a starting rate.** At width 384 the rule
gives $5 \times 10^{-4}$; at 768, $2.5 \times 10^{-4}$; at 384 wide and
24 layers, $2.5 \times 10^{-4}$. Under linear routing the ceiling is real
and its failure mode is measured: at a rate above it the validation loss
descends for some epochs and then rises to the mean-field plateau (about
0.06, the loss of predicting the field mean; a float32 error near 0.75),
and the checkpoint in that state routes every point of every block to a
single slice with all 256 anchors coincident, so the network can only emit
a per-case constant (@sec-nb-routingsat-verdict, measured on the plateaued
lanes themselves; first seen at width 512 in
@sec-nb-relframe-divergence-mechanism). @tbl-using-rate-ceiling shows the
measured edges: the rule rate is the best clean rate at every width and
depth tested, the ceiling falls at least as fast as 1/depth, and 48 layers
have no clean rate at all under linear routing.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-using-rate-ceiling
#| output: asis
import json
from pathlib import Path
C = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "cap435_reduction_2026-09-20.json"))["configurations"]
def cell(key):
    c = C[key]; m = c["pressure_l2_mean"]; seeds = c["pressure_l2_seeds"]
    if m is None: return "NaN / plateau"
    tag = "**" if m < 0.1 else ""
    return f"{tag}{m:.4f}{tag} ({', '.join(f'{s:.2f}' if s > 0.1 else f'{s:.4f}' for s in seeds)})"
rows = [
    ("384 wide, 12 layers", "5e-4", "1e-3", cell("isla|w384|d12|s256|lr1e-3"), "7.5e-4", cell("isla|w384|d12|s256|lr7.5e-4"), "5e-4", cell("isla|w384|d12|s256|lr5e-4")),
    ("768 wide, 12 layers", "2.5e-4", "5e-4", cell("isla|w768|d12|s256|lr5e-4"), "3.75e-4", cell("isla|w768|d12|s256|lr3.75e-4"), "2.5e-4", cell("isla|w768|d12|s256|lr2.5e-4")),
    ("384 wide, 24 layers", "2.5e-4", "5e-4", cell("isla|w384|d24|s256|lr5e-4"), "—", "—", "2.5e-4", cell("isla|w384|d24|s256|lr2.5e-4")),
    ("384 wide, 48 layers", "1.25e-4", "2.5e-4", "NaN / plateau", "—", "—", "1.25e-4", "NaN / plateau"),
]
out = "| configuration | rule rate | above the rule | error | between | error | at the rule | error |\n|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n"
for r in rows: out += "| " + " | ".join(r) + " |\n"
print(out)
print(": The learning-rate ceiling of linear routing, measured at 435 DrivAerML cars and 100,000 cells (the scaling budget), float32 at 500 epochs, "
      "surface-pressure error as the two-seed mean with the seeds in parentheses. A value near 0.75 is the mean-field plateau; bold values are clean "
      "training. How to read this: each row is one width and depth, and the three rate columns bracket its ceiling; the 48-layer row has no "
      "float32 value because the lane above the rule went to NaN and the lane at the rule reached the plateau after a clean start. "
      "It says nothing about cosine routing, which trained every one of these configurations cleanly at the higher rate (@sec-nb-routenorm-cars-verdict). "
      "Data: results/cap435_reduction_2026-09-20.json. {#tbl-using-rate-ceiling}")
```

At width 192 the window is 3e-4 to 1e-3 with 1e-3 best (3e-4 costs 8% in
500 epochs), the plateau between 1e-3 and 2e-3, and NaN at 1e-2
(@sec-robustness-lr, @sec-nb-ratewindow-verdict). Never run ISLA at the
recipe's GeoTransolver default of 3e-3; the ISLA configurations pin 1e-3
for that reason. The rule costs a centered control at the 512-wide corner
nothing, so it is a property of the routing parametrization, not a retuning
of the comparison (@sec-nb-corner-wlr-verdict, @sec-nb-cg-wlr-verdict).

**Cosine routing removes the ceiling on DrivAerML at no measured cost in
accuracy.** With `routing_norm: cosine` each block routes on the cosine
between the token state and a learned prototype per slice at a fixed
temperature, so every logit is bounded and no block can reach the one-slice
state however its weights grow. Tested at the rates that put linear routing
on the plateau (435 cars, 100,000 cells), every cosine lane trained cleanly
to epoch 500, including 768 wide at 1e-3 (four times the rule rate) and 48
layers at 2.5e-4 (a configuration linear routing could not train at any
rate); the routing probe finds at least 12 effective slices in every block,
and accuracy at the rule rates is within 1% of linear routing at widths 192
and 384 and 2% at 768 (@sec-nb-routenorm-cars-verdict). The best cosine
lanes are also the best ISLA lanes on that budget: 384 wide at 24 and 48
layers reach 0.0407 and 0.0406, the same floor GeoTransolver reaches at
1,024 wide (@fig-capacity). Under cosine routing, then, read the rule as
the rate to start from rather than a limit; the class default changes to
cosine once the same test on the wings reports.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why the linear-routing ceiling scales with width and depth"}
Each block's routing logits are an affine map of a normalized token state
whose weights are free to grow; a sharper routing concentrates the slice
states, which sharpens the next block's routing, and wider or deeper
networks raise the gain of that loop. The ceiling therefore falls like
1/width and at least 1/depth, and it is a property of the routing form, not
of the frame. Bounding the logits, as cosine routing does, breaks the loop:
the frame and head contracts are unchanged either way, and the plateau
state (every point in one slice, anchors coincident) becomes unreachable
(@sec-nb-routenorm-prereg).
:::

## Evaluation and the inference sampler {#sec-using-sampler}

**Score in float32 at the reporting protocol's 200,000 cells; when the cell
budget is fixed and smaller, draw the cells with the stratified sampler.**
Inference shares the training configuration and reads the checkpoint by run
identifier:

```bash
# sampling_resolution=200000 is the reporting protocol; the infer default is the whole mesh
python src/infer.py model=isla_surface dataset=drivaer_ml_surface \
    run_id=<the trained run_id> infer_split=val sampling_resolution=200000 precision=float32
```

Report in float32. The recipe trains under bf16 autocast, and every number
in this book is a float32 inference on the final-epoch checkpoint
(@sec-metrics). A bf16 inference differs from the float32 one by about 2%
of the prediction from rounding alone, and under a rigid motion of the
input its prediction moves by about 4% (pressure) and 7% (wall shear),
where the float32 prediction moves by 3e-5 (@sec-mt2-contracts). Where the
pose or the sampling-consistency contract is load-bearing, infer in
float32.

**For inference at a fixed cell budget, draw the cells with the stratified
sampler.** Replace the dataset's `SubsampleMesh` stage with the recipe's
`StratifiedSubsampleMesh`:

```yaml
    - _target_: ${dp:StratifiedSubsampleMesh}   # was SubsampleMesh
      n_cells: ${sampling_resolution}
```

It keeps the same inclusion law (every cell kept with probability $n/N$,
weight $N/n$), so nothing about the trained model or the quantity it
estimates changes, but the kept cells are a *systematic* draw along the
Morton order of the cell centroids (the ordering by interleaved coordinate
bits, a space-filling curve along which consecutive cells are spatial
neighbors), one per consecutive run of $N/n$ cells with a single random
offset. A systematic sample has the same expectation as
an independent draw for every cell-weighted integral and a lower variance
for smooth integrands. The effect is a free improvement for every model and
largest for ISLA, whose slice states are the noisiest estimates
(@sec-deficit-anatomy):

```{python}
#| label: tbl-using-strat
#| output: asis
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
RES = Path("..") / "results"
qv = json.load(open(RES / "quadvar_reduction_2026-09-17.json"))["arms"]
mean = statistics.mean
names = [("isla_ref", "ISLA"), ("gt_unit", "GeoTransolver"), ("transolver_unit", "Transolver")]
out = "| model | independent draw | stratified draw | change |\n|---|---:|---:|---:|\n"
for k, lab in names:
    a = qv[k]; u = a["unif"]["10000"]; ind = mean(u["seeds"]) if isinstance(u, dict) else u
    st = mean(a["strat"]["10000"]["seeds"])
    out += f"| {lab} | {ind:.4f} | {st:.4f} | {(st/ind-1)*100:+.1f}% |\n"
print(out)
print(": DrivAerML surface pressure (area-weighted relative L2, float32, 48 validation cars, 10,000 cells, seed means) "
      "for the same checkpoints under the independent and the stratified inference draw. How to read this: the change is "
      "an evaluation effect on fixed checkpoints; it does not alter the ranking of the models, only the size of the gap. "
      "Data: results/quadvar_reduction_2026-09-17.json. {#tbl-using-strat}")
```

The book keeps the independent draw for its headline comparisons and
reports the stratified draw as a labeled row (@sec-scoreboard); for a
deployment, use the stratified draw, or more cells.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="How many cells"}
Use the recipe default of 200,000 cells per case. The in-distribution gap
to GeoTransolver on DrivAerML at full data is present at the 10,000-cell
exploration budget (8%) and gone at 200,000, because most of it was
estimator variance in the slice states (@sec-deficit-anatomy); and the
error of every model is flat above 100,000 cells (@sec-scoreboard-tokens),
so nothing above the default buys accuracy. The fused geometry kernel, the
default on CUDA, keeps ISLA's step at a third of GeoTransolver's time and
memory at 200,000 cells (@sec-using-cost). If the budget forces fewer
cells, use the stratified draw.
:::

## Loading a trained model {#sec-using-checkpoint}

**A checkpoint carries its own constructor arguments, so loading is one
call and the forward call mirrors the recipe mapping.** A saved ISLA is a
PhysicsNeMo module checkpoint and loads with the class's `from_checkpoint`;
no configuration has to be repeated:

```python
from physicsnemo.experimental.nn import ISLA
model = ISLA.from_checkpoint("checkpoints/isla_surface.mdlus").eval()
out = model(points=x, normals=n, measure_weights=w, global_vectors=g_hat)  # (B, N, 1 + 3)
p, tau = out[..., :1], out[..., 1:]
```

`points` and `normals` are (B, N, 3), `measure_weights` (B, N) summing to the
surface area, `global_vectors` (B, 1, 3) or (B, 3) for one direction. The
output stacks the scalar fields first, then each vector field's three
components. For interior prediction with `isla_volume`, add `query_points`,
`query_normals` (the signed-distance gradient) and `query_scalars` (the signed
distance) and read the output at the query rows; deploy at the training query
count (200,000 at the reporting protocol), because the interacting decode's
prediction at a point depends on the joint query set
(@sec-interior-companion).

## Cost {#sec-using-cost}

**At the recipe dimensions ISLA and GeoTransolver have the same parameter
count; with the fused geometry kernel ISLA's training step matches
GeoTransolver's in time at half the memory up to 40,000 tokens and is a
third of it in both at 200,000 cells.** At those dimensions ISLA has 8.9M
parameters (GeoTransolver 9.0M). On
one GB300 in bfloat16, batch of one case, both models compiled as the
recipe runs them, the training step at 10,000 tokens is 47 ms at 1.30 GiB
with the geometry recompute on, against GeoTransolver's 45 ms at 2.70 GiB;
switching the recompute off gives 39 ms at 1.94 GiB. At 40,000 tokens the
default path is 119 ms against 53 ms and the fused kernel 52 ms at 4.5
against 10.0 GiB (@tbl-mt2-cost). Two practical consequences:

- **Leave `geo_checkpoint: true` unless you are short of time and long on
  memory.** It is bitwise identical in outputs and gradients.
- **Leave `geo_kernel` at its default (`null`).** On CUDA with one global
  vector the model selects the exact fused Triton kernel at the first forward
  pass (relative difference to the eager region at most $5.5 \times 10^{-7}$
  in bf16) and logs the choice; off CUDA, or with several global vectors, it
  falls back to the eager region. Force `eager` only to reproduce the exact
  arithmetic path of a checkpoint trained on the eager region.

The passive decoder adds 1.1M parameters and four read blocks; the
query-token interior configuration adds almost no parameters but spans every
token with the per-slice geometry, at 0.28 s per step and 6.0 GB at 10,000
interior queries (the exploration budget).

## Contracts you can check on your own data {#sec-using-contracts}

**Each contract is a one-line test on a loaded checkpoint, and a residual
far above float32 rounding points at the inputs, not the model.** The
contracts are exact properties of the code (@sec-mt2-contracts), and
each is cheap to verify on a loaded checkpoint: rotate and translate the
inputs by a random rigid motion and compare the scalars (unchanged) and the
vectors (rotated); scale the points by $k$ and the measure weights by $k^2$
(unchanged). In float32 the residuals are of order $10^{-5}$ on the
trained checkpoints; in bf16 autocast several percent, mostly rounding. A residual far above these on your own data means
the inputs, not the model: normals with inconsistent orientation, weights
that do not sum to the surface area, or positions that were already centered
or scaled by something sample-dependent before the model saw them. (The
model normalizes the normals and the global vectors itself, so their
magnitudes cannot cause a residual.)
